paras: The threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects took place in January 1882 in Lincoln County, Georgia, where Black men jailed on an accusation of trying to burn the house of P. A. Cox near Lincolnton were threatened with lynching. County officials kept the prisoners from the threatened lynching, though an Augusta dispatch said fear for their lives persisted.

According to news that reached Washington, Georgia, on a Sunday in late January, two attempts had been made the previous week to burn the residence of "Mr. Pleas. Cox" in Lincoln County. That report said five or six people were implicated, some of them Black and "one or two" white men, and that the plot was said to have been to burn the house and kill Cox as he came out.

Four Black men were arrested, and the Washington report stated that they "were threatened with lynching." An Augusta dispatch dated January 30 gave a fuller count: six "colored men" were arrested, three were discharged, and Harry Kennedy, John Horry and Henry Wright were held in prison. The dispatch described "considerable excitement" in the county and said that "the firmness of the county officials" had saved the prisoners from lynching.

F. H. Colley and M. P. Reese of Washington went to Lincoln County on a Monday to look into the matter. At the end of January, "apprehension" was still felt for the prisoners' lives, and no report of their trial or later fate appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News first noted the case in a single line of its "Georgia Affairs" column on January 26. The Augusta dispatch then ran on January 31 in Richmond, New York and Savannah, and on February 9 in Pickens, South Carolina, in nearly identical words. Headline writers framed the jailed men as the accused: the Savannah paper used "Threatened Lynching. Three Suspected House Burners in Peril," the New-York Tribune "Alleged Incendiaries in Danger," and the Richmond Dispatch simply "Excitement in Georgia." None of the copies named those who threatened the prisoners, and all credited the officials' "firmness" for preventing a lynching.

The Washington report counted four men arrested after two burning attempts, while the Augusta dispatch counted six arrested after one attempt; the earlier report may have preceded further arrests. The copies also differ on the distance from Lincolnton, four miles in most and five in the Pickens Sentinel, and on the spelling of Horry, given as "John Harvy" in Richmond.

No one was reported killed: the wire says the officials' firmness 'saved the prisoners from lynching' (A2, A4); the threat was tied to an accusation of house burning, but no group size is given.
A Washington, Ga., report (A1) and the separate Augusta wire (A2, A3, A4, A5) agree on an attempt to burn Cox's house, the arrest of Black men, and a threat to lynch them.

accounts.gist: Two attempts were made to burn Cox's house; five or six people, some negroes and one or two white men, were implicated; four negroes were arrested and threatened with lynching.

accounts.label: Augusta wire
accounts.gist: Six colored men were arrested over one attempt to burn Cox's house; three were discharged and three imprisoned, and county officials' firmness saved them from lynching.

framing.detail: Papers in Richmond, New York, Savannah and Pickens, S.C., ran the Augusta dispatch nearly verbatim, calling the prisoners 'suspected house burners' and 'alleged incendiaries' and crediting the officials' 'firmness'.
The Savannah 'Georgia Affairs' column reported the threat in one line among local items, repeating that the plot was 'said' to aim at killing Cox.
